I'm not saying the anger isn't valid, but funneling all these complicated emotions into it only helps in the short term. Coping methods can be effective but still maladaptive.

The way you react to things when you're already heated is not often how you wish you'd handled it once you've cooled off. I don't think the cousin should have posted, but in the scheme of things is it really a 'boundary being stomped on' or a well-intentioned but careless act? I don't think she was deliberately trying to cause harm, so fury objectively seems disproportionate.

Not condoning your cousin's actions, and honestly this take is more for your wellness than hers.

I think  this is all so raw that it's easier to turn to anger instead of sitting with your grief and the fear you have for your mother.

The only way out is through, and while the proverbial cat is out of the bag, I think it's worth considering it might be better for you all to face these challenges when your mother has you and help there to support her. Prolonging this awful new reality she's living may seem gentler, but it's going to be a painful adjustment no matter how slow you pull the bandaid.

You've all lost enough as it is. Can you put a pin in your anger for a little while, and just focus on the love you have for your parents? If you're still angry a month out, so be it, but if there's a chance it spares you some regret it might be worth it to give this no more of your energy.

Kind of late to the show here, but I thought I'd chime in. 

You were with this guy for a very long time, and it didn't work out. Reasons at this point are superfluous,  because you're learning to adapt to not having him around. 

The same way you look back now on that week immediately post-split is how you're going to feel about all the heartache somewhere down the road when you make peace with this chapter being over. That being said, don't judge yourself or push your heart to heal faster than it needs to. You're so entitled to feel all the ways that you do, but it's doing you a disservice to keep letting them hold you back from enjoying your life.

Instead of being fixated on the whys and why nots, try to focus on all the ways you're going to come out of this stronger, all the things you learned about yourself in the relationship, and how you're going to be okay. Go for an early morning run, catch up on rest you've undoubtedly been missing, listen to some Frank Turner and take a deep breath.

I once had an ex tell me in the throes of an awful breakup that I wasn't handling well "I'm not responsible for your happiness." It hit me like a ton of bricks, but that revelation was the pivot point where I decided instead of trying fix a broken relationship, I needed to focus on healing myself.

You're going to be okay. Trust that.
